cls: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) - active S-enantiomer of etodolac
quick: S-Etodolac 300 mg PO once or twice daily (single active enantiomer; about half the racemic dose)
Take with food or milk to reduce GI upset
Avoid, especially from 20 weeks (oligohydramnios) and contraindicated in third trimester
Avoid where possible; use the lowest dose for the shortest time
Avoid in significant renal impairment; risk of acute kidney injury
Use with caution; reduce dose in hepatic impairment
Blood pressure, renal function, hemoglobin/GI symptoms, liver enzymes
summary: S-Etodolac (dexetodolac) is the pharmacologically active S(+)-enantiomer of the NSAID etodolac, a pyranocarboxylic acid with preferential COX-2 inhibition. As the single active enantiomer it delivers the analgesic and anti-inflammatory effect of racemic etodolac at roughly half the dose, treating osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and acute pain. Like all NSAIDs it carries class risks of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events and gastrointestinal bleeding/ulceration/perforation, plus renal impairment and fluid retention. S-Etodolac is NOT FDA-approved as a separate product; this record is based on racemic etodolac labeling/SmPC and chiral-switch literature, with the single-enantiomer rationale noted.
indications: Management of acute pain (e.g., musculoskeletal pain, postoperative pain)

dosage.d: S-Etodolac 300 mg PO once or twice daily (lowest effective dose)
dosage.n: Approximately half the racemic etodolac dose; use lowest effective dose for shortest duration

dosage.d: S-Etodolac 200-300 mg PO every 8-12 hours as needed
dosage.n: Short-term use; do not exceed the equivalent maximum daily NSAID dose

dosage.d: Use the lowest effective dose; reduce in impairment
dosage.n: Avoid in significant renal impairment; monitor closely

admin: Take with food, milk or an antacid to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water; do not lie down for 10 minutes after dosing
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals
Ensure adequate hydration, particularly in the elderly or those at renal risk
Do not combine with other NSAIDs or take more than prescribed
moa: S-Etodolac is the active S-enantiomer of etodolac. It inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, with relative preference for COX-2, reducing synthesis of prostaglandins that mediate inflammation, pain and fever. The single-enantiomer formulation concentrates the activity in the pharmacologically active stereoisomer, allowing a lower total dose than the racemate while retaining anti-inflammatory and analgesic effect.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to etodolac or NSAIDs (including aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, urticaria, angioedema)
Setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery (peri-operative)
Active gastrointestinal bleeding or peptic ulceration
relative: History of peptic ulcer or GI bleeding
Cardiovascular disease or risk factors, hypertension, heart failure
Renal impairment, dehydration, concomitant diuretics/ACE inhibitors/ARBs
monitor: Blood pressure and signs of fluid retention

preg: NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy. Use after about 20 weeks' gestation may cause fetal renal dysfunction and oligohydramnios, and from around 30 weeks risks premature closure of the ductus arteriosus - so use is contraindicated in the third trimester. Avoid in earlier pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk; use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
lact: NSAIDs including etodolac are excreted in breast milk in small amounts. Where treatment is needed, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time; short-acting NSAIDs are generally preferred. Avoid in infants at particular risk and monitor the infant.
renal: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia. Avoid in significant renal impairment; in mild impairment use the lowest dose with monitoring of renal function, especially in volume-depleted patients or those on diuretics/ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
hepatic: Etodolac is extensively hepatically metabolised. Use with caution and consider dose reduction in hepatic impairment; avoid in severe impairment. Monitor liver enzymes, and discontinue if signs of clinically significant liver injury develop.

major: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel) - increased GI and bleeding risk
Other NSAIDs and systemic corticosteroids - additive GI ulceration/bleeding risk
Methotrexate - reduced clearance and increased toxicity (especially high-dose)
Lithium - reduced renal clearance, raised lithium levels
moderate: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics - reduced antihypertensive effect and increased risk of acute kidney injury (triple-whammy)
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; food may slightly delay absorption without reducing overall effect
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - increases the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false readings for urinary bilirubin/ketones and can mask fever; can elevate liver enzymes and affect renal function tests

serious: Serious cardiovascular thrombotic events (myocardial infarction, stroke)
Acute kidney injury and fluid retention / hypertension worsening
Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS)

monitoring: Blood pressure and signs of edema/heart failure
Renal function, especially in the elderly and those on diuretics/ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Hemoglobin and signs of GI bleeding with prolonged use
Liver enzymes periodically with long-term therapy
Cardiovascular risk reassessment for chronic use
counsel: Take with food and the lowest dose that controls your symptoms, for the shortest time
Stop and seek urgent care for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, chest pain, breathlessness, or sudden weakness/slurred speech
Avoid alcohol and do not take other anti-inflammatory painkillers at the same time
Tell your doctor if you have heart, kidney, liver, blood-pressure or stomach problems, or take blood thinners
Report any rash or blistering, swelling, or reduced urination promptly
pk: Analgesic onset within about 30 minutes to 1 hour
Plasma peak approximately 1-2 hours after oral dosing
Analgesia approximately 4-12 hours depending on dose/formulation
Store at room temperature 20-25 C; protect from moisture and light
pearls: S-Etodolac is the active S(+)-enantiomer of etodolac (a chiral switch); it is NOT FDA-approved as a separate product - this record is based on racemic etodolac labeling/SmPC and enantiomer literature
As the single active enantiomer it provides the racemate's effect at roughly half the dose, intended to reduce the inactive-enantiomer load
All NSAID class risks apply: serious cardiovascular thrombotic events and GI bleeding/ulceration/perforation (these carry boxed warnings for NSAIDs in the US)
Contraindicated peri-operatively for CABG and in the third trimester of pregnancy; avoid after 20 weeks due to fetal renal effects/oligohydramnios
Beware the 'triple whammy' of NSAID plus diuretic plus ACE inhibitor/ARB causing acute kidney injury
missed: If you take it on a schedule and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose - then skip it. Do not double up. If you use it only as needed for pain, take it when required without making up missed doses.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, and rarely seizures, renal failure, or metabolic acidosis. There is no specific antidote. Treat supportively: consider activated charcoal if ingestion was recent and substantial, protect the airway, monitor and support renal and cardiovascular function, and treat GI bleeding. Hemodialysis is of limited value due to high protein binding.
